evidence_quotes.quote: This study developed and tested an assessment tool to evaluate the compliance of households’ pit latrines and cesspits against RS ISO 24521 and identify factors associated with compliance.
Included households were only surveyed if they had a pit latrine or a cesspit.
The survey achieved a response rate of 93%, with 903 valid responses included in the analysis. Of these, 436 were households using pit latrines (48%), and 467 were households using cesspits (52%).

The demographic characteristics used as fixed effects in the GLMM are detailed in Table 1, and include Wealth of household, Residential type, Type of settlement, House tenure, Presence of piped water, and Age of the pit.

Sharing facilities was also significantly associated with house tenure, where shared pit latrines were more likely to be found among tenants in compounds and low-income households than in wealthier households, owning or living in single-family houses. This finding suggests the likelihood of reduced access to sanitation among households living in compounds and those who are tenants.

Among pit latrine users, 3.9% recommended regulating the responsibilities of landlords regarding sanitation services. This recommendation stems from challenges in delineating accountability for the operation and maintenance of shared latrines, including emptying, cleaning, and structural upkeep; issues that were closely linked to facility sharing, house tenure, and the physical condition of the pit latrine.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household onsite sanitation services (pit latrines and cesspits) in Kigali City, covering SDG 6.2 safely managed sanitation compliance, shared versus unshared household toilet access, affordability, and physical accessibility for fecal sludge emptying services (restricted to households that already had a pit latrine or cesspit).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, but fails the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading (plain_criterion2_decision = include; narrow decision = exclude, E03). Under the plain wording, the study references and measures regulatory/institutional elements: compliance against national standard RS ISO 24521 and RURA fecal sludge management guidelines, whether authorities ever conducted a sanitary inspection, respondent awareness of toilet construction regulations, master-planned (new) versus old settlements, and owner versus tenant housing tenure. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access is empirically examined: (1) all surveyed households already had a pit latrine or cesspit, and RS ISO 24521 is operationalized by the authors as a 26-item technical/hygienic facility quality scoring rubric (dependent variable) rather than a rule governing service eligibility or access; (2) house tenure (owning vs. renting) and Ubudehe wealth categories are standard household socio-demographic covariates, not legal documentation/tenure requirements or tariff/cost-recovery rules; (3) sanitary inspections by authorities and knowledge of construction regulations are sub-indicators embedded inside the environmental and sustainability compliance scores (and dropped in the refined tool as regards inspections) rather than analyzed as enforcement mechanisms governing service access; and (4) landlord accountability rules, subsidies, and stronger enforcement appear only as respondent/author policy recommendations.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence from a cross-sectional household survey, structured sanitation facility inspection, and direct observation of 903 households in Gasabo District, Kigali, analyzed using descriptive statistics, Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM), and Rao-Scott adjusted Chi-square tests.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes relevant to sanitation service access, availability, and affordability alongside structural/hygienic containment indicators, specifically unshared household facility status (37.4% for pit latrines, 92.5% for cesspits), facility affordability, emptying frequency and accessibility for emptying services, and overall safely managed compliance with RS ISO 24521 objectives.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (903 households/onsite facilities with pit latrines or cesspits in five sectors of Gasabo District), exposures (household socio-demographic/housing covariates and physical pit attributes), outcomes (binary full compliance and 26 indicator-level compliance measures), and cross-sectional survey/inspection study design.

study_design: Cross-sectional household survey, sanitation facility inspection, and direct observation analyzed with Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM) and Rao-Scott adjusted Chi-square tests
population_and_sample: 903 households using pit latrines (n = 436) or cesspits (n = 467) across five purposively selected sectors (Gisozi, Ndera, Rusororo, Kacyiru, Kimironko) of Gasabo District, Kigali City, out of 969 sampled households (unit of analysis: household / onsite sanitation facility)
exposure: Household socio-demographic and housing characteristics (Ubudehe wealth category, multi-household compound vs. single-family residential type, new master-plan vs. old settlement type, renting vs. owning house tenure, piped water in compound, pit age) and technical pit characteristics (sharing, pit condition, depth, emptying frequency, lining)
outcome: Compliance of household pit latrines and cesspits with four RS ISO 24521 standard objectives (Protection of Public Health, Meeting Needs and Expectations of Users, Sustainability, Protection of Environment) and 26 constituent indicators including unshared sanitation status, affordability, user satisfaction, safety, and emptying service accessibility and frequency
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) on the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Although this cross-sectional empirical survey of 903 households in Kigali examines household onsite sanitation outcomes (including unshared latrine access, affordability, emptying service accessibility, and compliance with RS ISO 24521), it only surveys households that already possess a pit latrine or cesspit and operationalizes RS ISO 24521 as a technical/hygienic facility quality scoring tool (dependent variable) modeled against household socio-demographic, housing occupancy (renting vs. owning), and physical pit characteristics. It does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements to obtain service, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, or regulatory enforcement governing access). Under the broad plain wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it assesses compliance with a national regulatory/technical standard and measures sanitary inspections, regulatory awareness, master-plan settlement status, and housing tenure.
